# Health-Journal Prose — Real Example Sentences by Section

Concrete companion to `health_journal_prose_style.md`. That file states the
conventions; this file **shows them**, using short sentences quoted from
published articles so the English has a real model to imitate — organised by the
section you are writing (Abstract · Introduction · Methods · Results ·
Conclusions · Recommendations), plus a sentence-craft appendix.

**How to use these.** Imitate the **structure and register** — where the number
sits, how the objective is phrased, how the hedge names its reason, how the
contrast turns — **never the content or wording**. These are other authors'
sentences about other studies; lifting a phrase into a new manuscript is
plagiarism. Write your own sentence about your own study in the same shape.

**Attribution & scope.** Each quotation is brief (one sentence), cited to its
journal and DOI, reproduced for style illustration (fair-use commentary); minor
OCR artefacts have been cleaned. Coverage is a curated sample from the reference
corpus (JAMA, JAMA Network Open, BMJ, *Lancet Digital Health*, *Nature* /
*Nature Medicine* / *npj Digital Medicine*, *World Psychiatry*, *Int. J. Nursing
Studies*), not an exhaustive set. Where a target journal's author instructions
differ, the journal governs; the claim-strength ladder and protected hedges
always apply (a style edit never moves a claim's strength).

---

## 1. Abstract

The header set is fixed by the journal family (see `health_journal_prose_style.md`
§8: JAMA = Importance/Objective/Design…/Main Outcomes/Results/Conclusions and
Relevance; BMJ = Objective/Design/…/Conclusions; Lancet = Background/Methods/
Findings/Interpretation/Funding; Nature/npj = unstructured). The abstract is
denser than the body and every number in it reappears in the body.

- **Findings (results element):** *"A total of 137 studies were included."*
  — JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- **Conclusions and Relevance:** *"In this systematic review of 137 chatbot
  health advice studies, the reporting quality was heterogeneous and may inform
  the development of the CHART reporting standards."* — JAMA Network Open
  (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- **Interpretation (Lancet abstract conclusion):** *"Our findings highlight the
  urgent need for comprehensive and transparent bias assessments of large
  language model tools such as GPT-4 for intended use cases before they are
  integrated into clinical care."* — Lancet Digital Health
  (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** the Findings line states the count plainly; the Conclusions
line opens by naming the **design and n** ("In this systematic review of 137 …")
and stops at the strength the results carry ("may inform"); the Interpretation
names the practical implication without overclaiming causation.

---

## 2. Introduction

Open on the **burden/importance**, then the **specific gap**, then a one-sentence
**objective**. Hedging here is about potential and importance, not findings.

- **Burden opener:** *"An estimated 970 million individuals live with mental
  health or substance use disorders worldwide, with depression and anxiety among
  the leading causes of disability-adjusted life years lost."* — World
  Psychiatry (doi:10.1002/wps.21352)
- **Scale of the technology/problem:** *"These tools perform millions of
  assessments annually, with about 7% of the German population using
  symptom-assessment apps."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **The gap (specific absence):** *"However, there is no evidence synthesis on
  the accuracy of large language models, and no review has contextualized the
  accuracy of symptom-assessment apps and large language models."* — npj Digital
  Medicine (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **Objective statement:** *"We aimed to assess whether GPT-4 encodes racial and
  gender biases that impact its use in health care."* — Lancet Digital Health
  (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)
- **Objective (alternative verb):** *"We sought to understand the medical
  comprehension, knowledge retrieval and reasoning capabilities of Med-PaLM."*
  — Nature (doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2)

**Why they work:** the burden sentence carries a concrete number and its source
of importance (DALYs); the gap is a *named* absence the study then fills, not a
vague "little is known"; the objective is a single "We aimed to / We sought to"
sentence naming the exposure/question and the outcome.

---

## 3. Methods

The most procedural section: past tense, both voices, almost no hedging and no
"However". Report search, screening, appraisal and synthesis in that order, and
give the **reason** for a method choice.

- **Search:** *"The seven databases were searched and 2432 articles were
  retrieved for review."* — Int. J. Nursing Studies
  (doi:10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2024.104991)
- **Registration:** *"Our protocol was prospectively registered on the Open
  Science Framework."* — JAMA Network Open
  (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- **Independent screening (the standard two-reviewer sentence):** *"The titles
  and abstracts were screened by two researchers independently; in cases of
  disagreement, both researchers re-examined the title and abstract and resolved
  conflicts through discussion."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **Eligibility by two reviewers (variant):** *"Each study was randomly assigned
  to at least two reviewers, who independently evaluated its eligibility based on
  predefined inclusion criteria."* — World Psychiatry (doi:10.1002/wps.21352)
- **Appraisal tool named:** *"Data extraction focused on basic study
  characteristics and conversational agent details, with the Cochrane Risk of
  Bias 2.0 tool employed for bias assessment."* — Int. J. Nursing Studies
  (doi:10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2024.104991)
- **Synthesis choice with its reason:** *"A narrative synthesis with no
  meta-analysis was planned, due to anticipated heterogeneity in study subjects
  and designs."* — JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)

**Why they work:** each names *what was done* in the past tense; the screening
sentence gives the reviewer count, independence, and the conflict-resolution
rule in one breath; the synthesis sentence states the choice **and why**
(heterogeneity) — the mark of a defensible Methods section.

---

## 4. Results

Lead with the pattern, then the number; keep interpretation out. Numbers carry
denominators and CIs.

- **Study flow:** *"A total of 1549 studies were screened and 19 included."*
  — npj Digital Medicine (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **Main effect as a range with CIs:** *"Performance on appropriate triage advice
  across the 23 individual symptom checkers ranged from 33% (95% confidence
  interval 19% to 48%) to 78% (64% to 91%) of standardized patient
  evaluations."* — BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj.h3480)
- **Effect range (concise):** *"The average accuracy of large language models
  ranged from 57.8% to 70.0%."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **Risk-of-bias result as n/N (%):** *"Most included studies (89%, 17 of 19) had
  at least one area with a high or unclear risk of bias."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **The contrastive turn inside Results:** *"However, GPT-4 did not consistently
  perform worse for any single demographic group across all cases."* — Lancet
  Digital Health (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** the estimate travels with its 95% CI in the same parentheses;
the range is anchored to a stated denominator ("standardized patient
evaluations"); the risk-of-bias line uses `n of N (%)`; no interpretation
intrudes. (BMJ CI style is "19% to 48%"; JAMA uses a comma, "19%-48%" — one per
paper.)

---

## 5. Conclusions

Restate what **this** study supports, opening on design + n, at the strength the
results carry. Novelty is bounded, not bare.

- *"Our findings indicate that symptom-assessment apps have a relatively low
  accuracy on average, but they also show that accuracy is highly dependent on
  the specific tool used."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- *"Our systematic review illustrates that conversational agent–based
  interventions were not only feasible and acceptable but also effective across
  various symptomatologies."* — Int. J. Nursing Studies
  (doi:10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2024.104991)
- *"Our findings highlight the need for consensus-based methods for evaluating
  large language models in health care."* — JAMA (doi:10.1001/jama.2024.21700)
- **Bounded novelty:** *"To the best of our knowledge, no study has
  systematically evaluated the impact of biases in GPT-4 for clinical
  applications."* — Lancet Digital Health (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** each attributes the claim to "Our findings / Our systematic
review", states it at measured strength (`indicate`, `illustrates`, `highlight
the need`), and — where novelty is claimed — bounds it ("to the best of our
knowledge"), never "this is the first".

---

## 6. Recommendations (implications for practice, policy and research)

Specific, derived from the findings and limitations, and proportionate to the
evidence. `Future research should…` is the corpus workhorse; practice/policy
recommendations are hedged to the evidence.

- **Research agenda:** *"Future research should prioritize rigorous clinical
  efficacy trials, transparent reporting of chatbot architecture, and ethical
  evaluations, to ensure that these technologies reliably enhance mental health
  care."* — World Psychiatry (doi:10.1002/wps.21352)
- **Research quality:** *"Future research should prioritize the methodological
  quality of randomized controlled trials to strengthen the evidence base
  supporting the use of conversational agents in symptom management."* — Int. J.
  Nursing Studies (doi:10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2024.104991)
- **Calibrated practice recommendation (neither over- nor under-claiming):**
  *"Based on the available evidence, the use of symptom-assessment apps or large
  language models should neither be universally recommended nor discouraged;
  rather, we suggest that their utility should be assessed based on the specific
  use case and user group."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- **Scope-of-use caveat:** *"Conversational agents should be viewed as
  complementary tools rather than replacements for traditional treatments,
  necessitating well-defined protocols for identifying and referring cases that
  require human intervention."* — Int. J. Nursing Studies
  (doi:10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2024.104991)
- **Policy/stakeholder:** *"Clinicians, patients, and regulators should be
  involved in collective efforts to agree and enforce appropriate deployment
  strategies for large language model technology in medicine."* — JAMA Network
  Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)

**Why they work:** the recommendation is specific ("prioritize … efficacy
trials, transparent reporting … ethical evaluations") and tied to the study's
own gap; the practice recommendation is explicitly bounded ("neither universally
recommended nor discouraged … assessed based on the specific use case"), which
matches observational or heterogeneous evidence rather than mandating action.

---

## 7. Sentence-craft appendix (cross-section)

**Titles — object + design after a colon:**
- *"Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study."*
  — BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj.h3480)
- *"Charting the evolution of artificial intelligence mental health chatbots from
  rule-based systems to large language models: a systematic review."* — World
  Psychiatry (doi:10.1002/wps.21352)

**The `However,` turn (one clean pivot, not stacked):**
- *"However, the generated output depends greatly on the initial input."*
  — JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- *"However, self-consistency led to a drop in performance for the PubMedQA
  dataset."* — Nature (doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2)

**Hedges that name their reason:**
- *"Second, the exclusion of multimodal tasks and basic biological science
  research might have led to an incomplete picture of large language model
  applications in health care."* — JAMA (doi:10.1001/jama.2024.21700)
- *"Although this improvement may seem small, the single-rater human performance
  on PubMedQA is 78.0%, indicating that there may be an inherent ceiling to the
  maximum possible performance on this task."* — Nature
  (doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2)

---

## 8. Putting it together — a short worked contrast

Weak (generic, could be any paper):

> "Our comprehensive analysis revealed that chatbots showed promising but
> concerning results, and it is important to note that further research is
> needed in this crucial area."

Rewritten in the corpus register (your own numbers, your own study):

> "Across the 12 studies, triage accuracy ranged from 41% to 88% (see Table 2).
> Accuracy was lower for emergency presentations, however, where under-triage
> could delay care. Because every study used vignettes rather than real patients,
> these estimates may not transfer to live use. Future research should test these
> tools with real patients before clinical deployment."

**What changed:** the vague intensifiers ("comprehensive", "promising but
concerning", "crucial", "further research is needed") are gone; the finding
leads with a number and denominator; the contrast turns once on `however`; the
hedge names the specific reason (vignettes, not real patients); and the
recommendation is specific and tied to that limitation.

---

**Epistemic status:** brief attributed quotations reproduced for style
illustration. They model English *structure*, not content — write your own
sentence about your own study.
